children: Ireland's central bank has raised its economic growth forecasts for 2026 and 2027 by around half a percentage point, citing stronger consumer spending and, in particular, a surge in AI-related investment by foreign multinationals.

The bank increased its forecast for the second successive quarter for modified domestic demand (MDD), its preferred measure of economic activity, to 3.8% in 2026 from 3.3% projected in June, and to 3.4% in 2027 from 2.8%.

Officials favour MDD because it strips out some of the distortions caused by Ireland's large multinational sector. MDD has grown strongly in recent years and accelerated to 4.7% in 2025, helped by the AI boom and Ireland's role as a major European data-centre hub.
GDP is still used to calculate Ireland's share of euro zone activity and can distort the bloc's outturn. The central bank forecast a 1.4% fall in Irish GDP this year and a 4.3% rebound in 2027.

Tariff-related stockpiling, particularly of weight-loss drug ingredients produced in Ireland by U.S. pharmaceutical companies, pushed Irish GDP up 12.3% in 2025 before it fell 7% so far this year as those stockpiles unwound.

Officials at Ireland's Central Statistics Office have also said the volatility reflects differences between how pharmaceutical companies value products held in inventory and the prices ultimately realised on export.

The central bank said on Wednesday that, according to Eurostat data, export volumes of weight-loss drug ingredients were little changed in the first half of 2026. However, the value of those exports fell to €0.5 billion from €42 billion in the same period last year.

Changes to how drug patents are handled, with greater patent value moving to the U.S., could explain the shift, Central Bank Director of Economics Robert Kelly said. He cautioned, however, that the data provided no concrete evidence of the reason.
A sustained drop in the value of such a large volume of exports could reduce corporate tax payments from the companies producing those drugs, Kelly added.

, which makes the active ingredient for its obesity drug Mounjaro in Ireland, is one of the country's biggest taxpayers. It paid $6.6 billion in corporate tax last year, 17% of all corporate tax receipts collected for 2025.
